Description: Environmental health science focuses on the link between the environment and human health. Environmental health science professionals serve on the front lines, protecting us from threats in our environment. They work to ensure the air we breathe, the water we drink, the food we eat and the communities we live in are safe. This is a STEM-based degree at the intersection of environmental science, chemistry, biology and public health. Our degree provides you with a strong scientific background to assess environmental problems and their effects on human health. Through our challenging curriculum and unique hands-on opportunities, we'll teach you the skills needed to create solutions to these complex problems. Our program is nationally accredited by the National Environmental Health Science and Protection Accreditation Council (EHAC), making us one of only 30 accredited undergraduate environmental health programs in the nation. This accreditation allows our graduates to enter the U.S. Public Health Service as commissioned officers. As part of the Institute for a Sustainable Environment, our students learn from and conduct research with expert faculty in a wide variety of areas. Our small class sizes allow our faculty to work one-on-one with students to meet their academic and career goals. We also work closely with our extensive alumni network to develop professional opportunities for our students. Through our interdisciplinary curriculum, you'll learn: The scientific principles behind major environmental problems, such as air pollution, water pollution and climate change. How environmental contaminants affect human health and the science of toxicology. The essential elements of epidemiology and how to investigate disease outbreaks. The principles of industrial hygiene and how to protect worker health and safety. How to apply risk assessment principles to evaluate and manage environmental health risks. The laws and policies that protect both environmental and public health. The hands-on skills to assess environmental quality and exposure in our state-of-the-art laboratories.

The Social Sciences major is the largest major in the Department of Humanities and Social Sciences. Its flexible degree requirements allow you to create an individualized course of study suited to your interests and career goals. Social science majors complete a minimum of one social science concentration. They are strongly encouraged to complete a second concentration, a minor, or a second major. Our students have paired the SS major with a second major in engineering, business, and the arts and sciences.

In a world of increasing complexity and rapid change, these are the transferable skills that employers and graduate schools demand. The research and analytical skills that you develop as a Social Sciences major will prepare you for careers in law, public policy, nonprofit management, market research, urban planning and a wide range of other professions. Description:
The social documentation major at Clarkson is an interdisciplinary program that teaches students how to use documentary storytelling techniques to represent the lived experiences of others, paying particular attention to the complex intersections of culture, society and politics. Students in this program will study the ethical, social and political dimensions of documentary work while also developing a set of practical skills in media production. We offer a mix of theoretical, historical and production-based coursework designed to help students think critically about the role of media in society and also participate in the production of media content in an informed way.

Social documentation majors learn to research, write, produce, direct, shoot and edit non-fiction films, and they learn how to think critically about the stories we tell through media. Students study the historical, theoretical and ethical dimensions of documentary film, and they gain a strong foundation in the use of contemporary production technologies to tell compelling and powerful stories. The social documentation curriculum is hands-on and project-based. Students will build a portfolio of documentary work that reflects their unique interests and career goals. Students have the opportunity to participate in one of our many off-campus study programs, including a popular semester-long program in New York City.

They study issues such as rural and urban life, the intersection of science and society, race and ethnicity, deviance and crime, gender roles and inequalities, and how institutions like education, government, healthcare, and religion shape our lives. Sociology provides an excellent liberal arts education and develops strong critical thinking, research, and communication skills applicable to a wide variety of careers in social work, public administration, law, business, education, policy analysis, advocacy, and counseling.

Description: Statistics is the science and art of learning from data. Statisticians offer essential insight into nearly every field imaginable, including business, science, technology, government and engineering. As a statistician, you'll apply mathematical and statistical knowledge to scientific, industrial and economic problems. Our statistics program will prepare you to enter the workforce with real-world skills and knowledge you can immediately put to use. Or you can continue your education with graduate study in statistics, actuarial science, business, economics or another related field. What you learn as a statistics major will also make you a more discerning consumer of information and a better-informed citizen. Our program will train you in the theory and practice of statistics. Throughout our program, you'll learn to be a strong communicator, both orally and in writing. Description: The Bachelor of Science in War and Peace Studies at Clarkson University is a new, innovative major that examines one of the most fundamental problems of human existence: the organized use of violence. Why do humans go to war? Are there certain conditions that make war more or less likely? How has warfare changed over time and how is it likely to change in the future? What are the human, economic, and political costs of war? What can we learn from past wars? What are the essential components of a just and lasting peace? This interdisciplinary major will train you to become a critical thinker about issues related to war, peace, security, and global affairs. Our core curriculum combines history, social science, and humanities. You'll take courses on military history, the sociology of war and peace, the politics of security, and the ethics of war. The minor is comprised of five courses, with a requirement that at least three courses are taken outside of the student's major requirements. In addition to a set of three required core courses that build a strong foundation, students have the opportunity to take specialized elective courses on topics like pollution prevention, sustainable development, industrial ecology, and water resources engineering.

Through this program, you will not only gain a stronger understanding of the technical aspects of environmental engineering, but will also have an appreciation for the social, political and economic complexities that are often inherent in environmental decision-making.

ProgramName: Minor in Sustainable Solutions for Small Island Communities
Requirements:
Students in the minor in sustainable solutions for small island communities must complete a minimum of 18 credit hours, including 12 credits of core courses and 6 credits of electives. The core courses will give you a fundamental introduction to both the complex challenges facing these communities and the interdisciplinary approaches to problem-solving. Through your electives, you will tailor your knowledge to a particular area of interest, like environmental health or policy. You may not use courses that are required for your major to satisfy the requirements for this minor.

Required Courses (12 credits):
EV102 - Introduction to Sustainability for Small Island Communities
EV202 - Culture and Environment of Small Island Communities
EV302 - Case Studies in Sustainable Development for Small Island Communities
EV402 - Senior Design in Sustainable Development for Small Island Communities

Technical Electives (6 credits), select two from the following:
ANTH365 - Global/Local Issues in Food
BY314 - Tropical Biology and Ecology
CE340 - Water & Wastewater Treatment
CE479 - Water Resources Engineering
EHS309 - Global and Public Health
ES330 - Introduction to Ecology
ES340 - Environmental Chemistry
ES432 - GIS
ES436 - Ecological Economics & Policy
EV311 - Sustainable Agriculture
POL360 - Environmental Policy & Politics
SS232 - Environment & Society
Description: Small island communities around the globe are facing many serious challenges to their long-term sustainability. These communities are often on the front lines when it comes to the impacts of climate change, including extreme weather events, sea level rise and ocean acidification. These communities are also often located in remote areas, with a small economic base and rely on long supply chains for food, energy and manufactured goods. The combination of these factors makes these communities extremely vulnerable to the predicted effects of climate change and other global disturbances (such as a global pandemic or other disruptions to global trade). The Minor in Sustainable Solutions for Small Island Communities is a 15-credit minor that aims to provide students with foundational knowledge of the unique sustainability challenges faced by small island communities, including those in the developing world and indigenous communities. Students will learn the key principles of sustainability and sustainable development, gain a technical understanding of the key environmental issues facing these communities and develop skills that are required to identify and help implement sustainable solutions in the areas of water, energy, food and waste. This minor is open to all Clarkson undergraduate majors.
ProgramWebsiteURL: The official university website for Clarkson University is https://www.clarkson.edu.

ProgramName: Minor in War and Peace Studies
Description: War and peace studies is an interdisciplinary minor designed to examine the causes of war and the conditions necessary for peace. The program is specifically concerned with military force and its effects on society. The minor covers a wide variety of topics, including international conflict, military history, the role of intelligence and national security, civil-military relations, terrorism, arms control, and defense policy. The study of war and peace can prepare you for a career in federal service as a civilian or military employee in the Department of Defense, the Department of State, the National Security Council or the intelligence community. The minor may also be helpful in pursuing a business career with defense contractors or other internationally oriented firms, or in a variety of non-governmental organizations.
